questions.q: Which of the following is the support function $h_K$ of a convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$?
questions.explain: By definition $h_K(u)=\sup_{x\in K}\langle u,x\rangle$. Then $K=\bigcap_u\{x:\langle u,x\rangle\le h_K(u)\}$ recovers $K$ from $h_K$.
questions.hint: The supporting hyperplane lives on the side where $\langle u,x\rangle$ is largest.

questions.q: Which of the following must be true for a convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ (compact convex with non-empty interior)?
choices: Every boundary point has at least one supporting hyperplane.
questions.explain: Hahn–Banach guarantees a supporting hyperplane at every boundary point. Homogeneity and subadditivity are immediate from the sup definition. Convex bodies need not have finitely many extreme points — a Euclidean ball has uncountably many.
questions.hint: Three are general convex-body facts; one is a polytope-only property.

questions.q: Let $K=[-1,1]^2\subset\mathbb{R}^2$ and $u=(\cos\theta,\sin\theta)$. Compute $h_K(u)$ when $\theta=\pi/4$ (give the value to 3 decimals).
questions.explain: $h_K(u)=\sup_{|x_1|,|x_2|\le 1}(x_1\cos\theta+x_2\sin\theta)=|\cos\theta|+|\sin\theta|$. At $\theta=\pi/4$ this is $\sqrt 2\approx 1.414$.
questions.hint: Maximise $x_1\cos\theta+x_2\sin\theta$ over $|x_i|\le1$ independently.

questions.q: Let $B\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be the unit ball and $K$ a convex body. The Steiner formula expands $\mathrm{vol}(K+\varepsilon B)$ as a polynomial in $\varepsilon$. What is the coefficient of $\varepsilon$ to leading order?
questions.explain: Differentiating $\mathrm{vol}(K+\varepsilon B)$ at $\varepsilon=0$ gives the surface area of $K$; the mixed-volume form $n\,V(K,\ldots,K,B)$ is the same number, since the Steiner polynomial expands $\mathrm{vol}(K)+\varepsilon\,\mathrm{surf}(K)+O(\varepsilon^2)$.
questions.hint: The first-order term measures how fast volume grows when you grow $K$ by an $\varepsilon$ shell.

questions.q: Let $A=[0,2]\times[0,1]$ and $B=[0,1]\times[0,3]$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$. Compute $\mathrm{vol}(A+B)$.
questions.explain: $A+B=[0,3]\times[0,4]$, so $\mathrm{vol}(A+B)=3\cdot 4=12$. Note this is larger than $\mathrm{vol}(A)+\mathrm{vol}(B)=2+3=5$.
questions.hint: For rectangles the Minkowski sum is the rectangle of summed widths.

questions.q: The mixed volume $V(K_1,\ldots,K_n)$ of $n$ convex bodies in $\mathbb{R}^n$ is best described as...
choices: the volume of the intersection $K_1\cap\cdots\cap K_n$
the unique symmetric multilinear function of $K_1,\ldots,K_n$ whose diagonal $V(K,\ldots,K)=\mathrm{vol}(K)$
the volume of the Cartesian product $K_1\times\cdots\times K_n$
questions.explain: Mixed volumes are defined precisely as the symmetric polynomial coefficients in $\mathrm{vol}(\lambda_1 K_1+\cdots+\lambda_n K_n)$; symmetry, multilinearity in Minkowski sum, and the normalisation $V(K,\ldots,K)=\mathrm{vol}(K)$ characterise them uniquely.
questions.hint: Think of $V$ as the multilinear version of $\mathrm{vol}$.

questions.q: Brunn–Minkowski states $\mathrm{vol}(A+B)^{1/n}\ge\mathrm{vol}(A)^{1/n}+\mathrm{vol}(B)^{1/n}$. When does equality hold for convex bodies $A,B$?
choices: Always (the inequality is in fact an equality).
Iff $A$ and $B$ are homothetic — $B=\lambda A+v$ for some $\lambda>0$ and $v\in\mathbb{R}^n$.
questions.explain: Equality holds precisely when $A$ and $B$ differ by a translation and a positive scaling. Balls are a special homothetic family but not the only one.
questions.hint: Translating $B$ and uniformly scaling it doesn't change the geometry of the pair.

questions.q: Take $A=B$ the unit ball $B^n$ in $\mathbb{R}^3$. Brunn–Minkowski compares $\mathrm{vol}(A+B)^{1/3}$ to $\mathrm{vol}(A)^{1/3}+\mathrm{vol}(B)^{1/3}$. What is the ratio LHS/RHS?
questions.explain: $A+B=2B^3$, so $\mathrm{vol}(A+B)=2^3\mathrm{vol}(B^3)$ and $\mathrm{vol}(A+B)^{1/3}=2\,\mathrm{vol}(B^3)^{1/3}$, exactly equal to the RHS. This is the equality case (homothetic with $\lambda=1$).
questions.hint: $A+A=2A$ for any convex $A$ in the Minkowski sense.

questions.q: Which classical inequality follows from Brunn–Minkowski by taking $B=\varepsilon B^n$ and expanding to first order in $\varepsilon$?
choices: The isoperimetric inequality on $\mathbb{R}^n$: among bodies of equal volume, the ball minimises surface area.
questions.explain: The first-order Steiner expansion turns Brunn–Minkowski into $\mathrm{surf}(K)\ge n\,\omega_n^{1/n}\,\mathrm{vol}(K)^{(n-1)/n}$, with equality iff $K$ is a ball — exactly the Euclidean isoperimetric inequality.
questions.hint: Think of $K+\varepsilon B$ as an $\varepsilon$-tubular neighbourhood.

questions.q: For a tetrahedron in $\mathbb{R}^3$ the $f$-vector is $(f_0,f_1,f_2)=(4,6,4)$. Compute the alternating sum $f_0-f_1+f_2$.
questions.explain: $4-6+4=2$. Euler's relation in $n=3$ gives $f_0-f_1+f_2=2$ (i.e. $1-(-1)^3=2$). Every 3-polytope has this sum equal to 2, matching the Euler characteristic of $S^2$.
questions.hint: Euler's relation: $\sum(-1)^i f_i=1-(-1)^n$.

questions.q: The Minkowski–Weyl theorem says a subset $P\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is a polytope iff...
choices: $P$ is the intersection of finitely many half-spaces and unbounded.
$P$ is the convex hull of finitely many points; equivalently, $P$ is a bounded intersection of finitely many half-spaces.
$P$ has finitely many extreme points and is closed.
$P$ is the unit ball of some norm on $\mathbb{R}^n$.
questions.explain: Minkowski–Weyl is the equivalence of the V-representation (convex hull of vertices) and the H-representation (intersection of half-spaces), for bounded sets.
questions.hint: Two equivalent descriptions: vertices vs. half-spaces.

questions.q: A polytope $P\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ is called simple when...
choices: every facet has the same number of vertices
every vertex lies on exactly $n$ facets
questions.explain: Simple polytopes have each vertex meeting exactly $n$ facets (equivalently, $n$ edges). The dual notion — every facet is a simplex — defines simplicial polytopes.
questions.hint: Don't confuse simple with simplicial: the two are polar-dual.

questions.q: For a centrally symmetric convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$, John's theorem says the maximal inscribed ellipsoid $E$ satisfies which inclusion?
questions.explain: For symmetric $K$, John's inclusion is $E\subseteq K\subseteq\sqrt n\,E$. The non-symmetric version weakens the factor to $n$. The factor $\sqrt n$ is saturated by the cross-polytope and the cube.
questions.hint: Symmetry buys a square-root factor.

questions.q: The Banach–Mazur distance between the cube $[-1,1]^n$ and the cross-polytope $\{x:|x_1|+\cdots+|x_n|\le 1\}$ in $\mathbb{R}^2$ is $d=\sqrt 2$. Give this to 3 decimals.
questions.explain: Both bodies have their inscribed John ellipsoid matching a Euclidean disk up to a factor of $\sqrt 2$ on either side, giving $d=\sqrt 2\approx 1.414$. In general, $d(\text{cube}_n,\text{cross-polytope}_n)=\sqrt n$ — saturating John's bound.
questions.hint: These two bodies are polar duals; their distance saturates John.

questions.q: The set of $n$-dimensional normed spaces modulo isometry, equipped with the Banach–Mazur distance, is...
choices: a compact metric space (the Banach–Mazur compactum) of finite diameter — $\le n$ in general, $\le\sqrt n$ for symmetric bodies
questions.explain: John's theorem implies every $n$-dim norm is within Banach–Mazur distance $\le\sqrt n$ of $\ell^2_n$, so the compactum has finite diameter; it is also compact (Auerbach + a precompactness argument).
questions.hint: John's inclusion is exactly a diameter bound on this space.

questions.q: Let $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ be a closed convex body containing the origin. What is $(K^\circ)^\circ$?
choices: $K^\circ$ — the polar is its own polar.
$-K$ — the reflection of $K$ through the origin.
$K$ — the bipolar theorem says polarity is an involution.
questions.explain: The bipolar theorem: for closed convex $K$ containing $0$, $(K^\circ)^\circ=K$. (For general sets one takes the closed convex hull of $K\cup\{0\}$.)
questions.hint: Polar duality is order-reversing and an involution.

questions.q: In $\mathbb{R}^2$ the unit square $K=[-1,1]^2$ has $\mathrm{vol}(K)=4$. Its polar $K^\circ=\{y:|y_1|+|y_2|\le1\}$ is the cross-polytope with $\mathrm{vol}(K^\circ)=2$. Compute $\mathrm{vol}(K)\cdot\mathrm{vol}(K^\circ)$.
questions.explain: $4\cdot 2=8$. Mahler's conjecture predicts $\mathrm{vol}(K)\mathrm{vol}(K^\circ)\ge 4^n/n!=16/2=8$ in dimension 2 for symmetric $K$ — the cube–cross-polytope pair achieves equality. Mahler's conjecture is proven for $n\le 3$.
questions.hint: The polar of the cube is the cross-polytope, and vice versa.

questions.q: Bourgain's hyperplane (slicing) conjecture asks: does there exist a universal $c>0$ such that every centrally symmetric convex body $K\subset\mathbb{R}^n$ of volume 1 has some hyperplane section of volume...
questions.explain: The conjecture asserts a dimension-free lower bound on the maximal hyperplane section: $\sup_{H}\mathrm{vol}(K\cap H)\ge c$. The best known bound is $\Omega(1/\log n)$ (Klartag, 2024), down from Bourgain's original $\Omega(n^{-1/4})$.
questions.hint: The conjecture forbids 'all sections are tiny'.

questions.q: Dvoretzky's theorem says every centred $n$-dim convex body has an almost-Euclidean section of dimension $k$ growing like...
questions.explain: Dvoretzky–Milman: $k=\Omega(\varepsilon^2\log n)$ for $(1+\varepsilon)$-Euclidean sections. The bound is tight up to constants (cube and cross-polytope saturate logarithmic growth).
questions.hint: Spherical concentration gives only a log-dimensional almost-round subspace.

questions.q: Milman's proof of Dvoretzky's theorem hinges on...
choices: concentration of measure on the sphere $S^{n-1}$
questions.explain: Milman established Lévy's lemma on $S^{n-1}$ for Lipschitz functionals and applied it to the norm restricted to a random subspace. Concentration of measure is the engine; Hahn–Banach (existence of supporting hyperplanes) is upstream of the convex-body setup but doesn't power the section result.
questions.hint: What makes random directions look uniformly the same?

questions.q: Which statements are true consequences or close cousins of Dvoretzky's theorem?
choices: Every $n$-dim normed space has an almost-isometric $\Omega(\log n)$-dim subspace isomorphic to Hilbert space.
The original motivation of Dvoretzky was a question of Grothendieck on $\ell^2$-like subspaces of Banach spaces.
Every convex body is itself an ellipsoid.
John's theorem: every centred convex body has a unique maximal inscribed ellipsoid.
questions.explain: Items 1 and 2 are direct restatements of Dvoretzky and its historical motivation. John's theorem is a closely related convex-geometric fact about ellipsoidal approximation. Item 3 is false — most convex bodies are far from ellipsoids; Dvoretzky only guarantees an almost-ellipsoidal section.
questions.hint: Dvoretzky finds a round subspace, not a round body.
